analysis.headline: Orakl Oncology's $34M Series A for tumour-organoid trial forecasting led a light evening alongside a $5.3M blood-biomarker pre-seed and BioMap's no-terms partner slate, so the week's big money is still Third Rock–Funnel (up to ~$2.16B) and argenx–Unnatural Products ($550M cash) ahead of Anthropic's Nov 18 IPO pricing
analysis.summary: The largest deals of the past week remain back-loaded: Funnel's pact with Third Rock heads the list on headline value (up to ~$2.16B, no upfront disclosed), while argenx is paying $550M in cash for Unnatural Products (up to ~$1.15B). Anthropic's IPO prices Nov 18 at $70 to $78 (up to about $1.02T on outstanding shares, about $1.4T fully diluted) and Isomorphic's reported ~$5B at ~$50B is still unclosed. Disclosed bio×AI venture since Oct 22 is now about $635M (Pathos $237M, Warp $215M, Hexagon $62M, Opentrons $40M, Orakl $34M, Biomatter $18M and smaller rounds); Proximal Ventures' $27.5M fund is fund capital and not counted.

themes.title: AI labs move from vendor to drug owner, and design platforms find new kinds of buyers
themes.detail: Anthropic's S-1 sells drug discovery and lab-running models to public investors, and on Nov 10 it set a $70 to $78 range implying up to about $1.02T on outstanding shares (about $1.4T fully diluted); the company owns Mithril's muscular-dystrophy antibodies with candidates planned for 2027, and its drug R&D head now puts its pipeline at two to five preclinical programs. OpenAI bought Orchestra Bio and backs Chai and Biossil, the $1B drug-repurposing startup whose $153M round its fund led and which signed its first asset buy on Nov 2; Anthropic's Anthology Fund joined Basecamp's $140M. Generate Biomedicines' Q3 report (Nov 12) confirms a research collaboration with Anthropic on agentic CAR-T design, in which Claude helped shrink a key CAR component by about 70%. Former OpenAI staff founded Warp ($215M) and another is reportedly raising about $200M. Startups are getting the same pipeline-wide access: Pfizer is putting Edison Scientific's Kosmos agent to work on its internal data across oncology, immunology and internal medicine. Alphabet's Isomorphic is now reportedly in talks for about $5B at around $50B, up from $2B+ at $40B+ in October, with first human trials said to be targeted around year-end. Buyers of AI design are widening beyond pharma: Third Rock Ventures, a company-creation venture firm, signed up to about $2.16B with Beijing's Funnel Biosciences for de novo antibodies against targets it chooses, its second such pact with a Chinese AI shop after Perpetual Medicine. At the small end, platforms are changing hands for stock: on Nov 10 Rakovina licensed Artemis.AI for its DNA-repair cancer targets for C$1M in shares and no cash, after iSpecimen's mostly-stock FoldLab purchase the week before.

themes.title: AI moves into trial design, recruitment and clinical assets
themes.detail: In one week Boehringer and Microsoft agreed to test digital patient twins, AstraZeneca and Oracle signed a term sheet for AI trial recruitment, Atlas Bio raised a $10M seed to simulate Phase II trials, adsilico raised £10M to test medical devices on AI-built virtual patients, and BMS is using Claude to judge trial plans. Formation Bio went further, raising $600M to buy Phase 1–2 drugs and run them through its AI-native development platform, and Pathos's $237M also funds AI-led trials. Upstream of the clinic, AstraZeneca is also testing Tremont AI's toxicology-pathology models to speed preclinical safety reads. Biossil is running the same buy-don't-discover play at a smaller scale, picking up Theriva's paused Phase 1b/2a transplant-gut enzyme for $350K upfront and up to ~$91M in milestones. The services layer is drawing its own seed money too: on Nov 10 Proximal Ventures closed a $27.5M debut fund, backed by SignalFire and Kleiner Perkins, for startups automating the development work pharma outsources. Digital twins are reaching obesity too: on Nov 12 Unlearn said it is modelling untreated outcomes for Structure Therapeutics' oral GLP-1 extension study, with results at ObesityWeek (Nov 14–17). On Nov 12 Paris-based Orakl Oncology raised a $34M Series A, co-led by Norrsken VC and Singular with Bpifrance's patient fund joining, to forecast cancer-trial outcomes from patient tumour organoids plus clinical records, with four Sanofi assets as its first live test; a day earlier Switchpoint Bio raised a $5.3M pre-seed for AI-read blood methylation tests that track treatment response.

themes.title: Make, test and manufacture: money for the physical layer
themes.detail: Warp ($215M, chemistry robots), Multiply Labs ($75M, robotic biomanufacturing), Opentrons ($40M Series E for AI-driven benchtop robots already in most top-20 pharma labs), Xaira's X-Automate and Rivercell (€22M) all bet the bottleneck has moved from design to the lab. Danaher is building NVIDIA AI into its instruments for closed-loop experiments, and Anthropic's filing talks about models running lab robots. UCB's Nov 4 deal with Cradle and Roche's Nov 5 deal with Chai are the software side of the same split: pharma keeps the wet lab and licenses the design models (Cradle's retrain on each batch of UCB results; Chai-3 goes across Roche's discovery programs). The Nov 9 argenx deal puts a price on a working make-and-test loop: $550M in cash for machine learning tied to massively parallel peptide synthesis and direct-to-biology screening, bought by a partner that had watched it run for more than two years. XtalPi's Pierre Fabre deal the same day also sells AI and robotics as one package. Automation is also reaching the cell supply itself: on Nov 10 Mitsui Chemicals took a stake in iORGANBIO, which makes human cells and organoids for drug testing in a closed loop of AI, single-cell readouts and robots, and will co-develop culture conditions with it. Revenue-stage protein design is following the same playbook: Biomatter's $18M Series A (Nov 12), led by Astanor, pays for a 2,000 m² Vilnius design-and-test site to shorten enzyme design cycles for customers that include AstraZeneca and Sanofi. Chinese platforms are bundling the same way: BioMap's Nov 12 partner slate, with no terms, includes MegaStream TechBio, an automated closed-loop discovery venture with Harbour BioMed, and an AI biomanufacturing lab with Revvity.

themes.title: Scale of data over number of platforms: big tech and pharma pay for the data layer, and investors now fund simulated data and physics too
themes.detail: Google DeepMind, Isomorphic and Meta put $300M into Biohub's $1.8B open virtual-cell data coalition alongside DOE and NIH, and days later GSK, Pfizer and Sanofi became founding partners in Parse and Nomic's Cascade, a licensed 100M-cell immune perturbation dataset with matched protein readouts. Flagship merged three single-platform companies into Etcelera around a 150M-cell foundation model, BioGeometry raised past $100M to pair its design model with a virtual cell model and an automated lab, and ALLOX, Rivercell and now Venomics AI ($2.7M pre-seed for a venom-molecule atlas) raised early rounds to generate their own experimental data. Buyers now pay for data at scale, split into an open track (Biohub) and a closed, pharma-shared track (Cascade), which squeezes startups selling a proprietary atlas on its own. A third track appeared on Nov 5: Potential Sciences raised an eight-figure seed, co-led by the UK's Sovereign AI fund, to train chemistry models on physics-based quantum calculations run on GPUs instead of lab data. Fathom Therapeutics, which simulates protein motion with physics plus AI and counts Lilly Ventures among its backers, added Greek-American fund Kos to a Series A now put at $55M on Nov 6, a second physics-first chemistry bet in two days. Data holders outside pharma are starting to trade data for a share of the drugs rather than a fee: on Nov 9 Korean genomics firm 3billion put the genomes from its rare-disease testing business behind DeepLife's TwinCell virtual-cell model to co-develop small molecules against genetic modifier targets. Open-model companies are buying measured data too: on Nov 11 Boltz said it now trains the ADMET models in its BoltzMol-1 product on Excelra's curated GOSTAR solubility, lipophilicity and permeability measurements, on undisclosed terms.

movers.direction: From models to owning life-sciences workflows, and now backing clinical-asset buyers
movers.detail: OpenAI bought Orchestra Bio to put pharma-operations agents into Rosalind and is an investor in Chai, which added Roche on Nov 5 after GSK in October. It also works with Formation Bio (with Sanofi), which just raised a $600M drug-acquisition fund. Alumni are spinning out bio companies: Kevin Weil's Warp, and Miles Wang reportedly raising about $200M. Its startup fund led Biossil's $153M round at a reported $1B, and Biossil has started buying shelved clinical drugs (Theriva's SYN-004 on Nov 2).

movers.direction: From selling Claude to pharma to owning drug programs, now part of its IPO story
movers.detail: Anthropic's S-1 (Oct 26) frames drug discovery and model-run labs as core uses and names Novo Nordisk, BMS, AbbVie and Sanofi as customers. It disclosed buying Mithril Medicine in July (after Coefficient Bio this spring), is taking its rare-disease antibodies toward candidates in 2027, and its drug R&D head describes two to five active preclinical programs; its Anthology Fund joined Basecamp's $140M. The $70 to $78 range (up to $64.4B plus a $26B private placement) puts it at up to about $1.02T on outstanding shares or about $1.4T fully diluted, with pricing set for Nov 18 and trading Nov 19. Per Forbes (Nov 11) it now runs a San Francisco wet lab and intends to hand clinical trials to pharma partners rather than run them itself. Generate Biomedicines' Q3 report (Nov 12) lists a research collaboration with Anthropic on agentic CAR-T design, terms undisclosed.

movers.direction: Into clinical development through pharma partnerships
movers.detail: Microsoft is testing digital patient twins and synthetic control arms with Boehringer Ingelheim, and Oracle signed a term sheet with AstraZeneca to use hospital data and AI for trial recruitment. Cloud vendors are pitching at the trial stage, while Google's Isomorphic stays in discovery. Specialists are taking the same tools to smaller sponsors: Unlearn's Nov 12 digital-twin analysis for Structure Therapeutics' oral GLP-1.

movers.direction: Scaling capital toward a $50B valuation and buying early access to biology's training data
movers.detail: Isomorphic is reportedly in talks to raise about $5B at roughly $50B (Bloomberg, Nov 4), up from $2B+ at $40B+ a month earlier, which would take outside funding to about $7.7B. It has a data-access roadmap with Abu Dhabi's health department, and with Google DeepMind and Meta put $300M into Biohub's $1.8B open cell-data coalition, reportedly with a one-year head start on the data.

movers.direction: In the cap tables and now inside lab instruments
movers.detail: NVentures joined Basecamp's $140M Series C, NVIDIA-backed Iambic raised $150M in its IPO, and Danaher is building NVIDIA computing and BioNeMo models into its lab instruments. NVIDIA rarely leads, but it now spans model companies, public drug developers and lab hardware. It is also supplying compute in kind to Biohub's virtual-cell coalition.

movers.direction: Licensing AI platforms for delivery, and holding equity in AI biologics developers
movers.detail: Lilly signed METiS for AI-designed lipid nanoparticles (low double-digit millions upfront, up to $1.1B), adding to its run of AI deals this year. Lilly Ventures is also in Fathom Therapeutics' $55M Series A for physics-plus-AI small-molecule design, which added Kos as an investor on Nov 6. Its older AI-target bets are paying out in steps: on Nov 11 Fauna Bio named a second obesity target from its hibernator-genomics platform under their 2023 pact (up to $494M in milestones), triggering an undisclosed payment.

movers.direction: Spreading AI bets from discovery through preclinical safety to trials, plus manufacturing robots and Gulf trial capacity
movers.detail: AstraZeneca signed insitro for MASH and cardiomyopathy targets, a term sheet with Oracle for AI trial recruitment (starting in Abu Dhabi with M42), a research deal with Tremont AI for AI-read preclinical toxicology, invested in Multiply Labs' $75M round, partners with Pathos on an ER PROTAC and is exploring up to 30 trials in Abu Dhabi by 2030.

movers.direction: Buying equity and access in AI for neurology and trial planning
movers.detail: BMS led Pathos's $237M Series E, with Alzheimer's as the first focus, and is using Anthropic's Claude to assess early trial plans, with wider work planned for 2027.

movers.direction: Buying its way beyond antibodies with an ML-guided oral peptide platform
movers.detail: After more than two years of collaboration and a minority stake, argenx is paying $550M in cash and up to $595M in milestones for Unnatural Products, which will become its peptide discovery hub. It follows the $2.2B Forte Biosciences purchase in July, which was not an AI deal.

movers.direction: Buying AI scientists and shared training data rather than owning AI companies
movers.detail: In one week Pfizer signed Edison Scientific to run its Kosmos agent on internal data across oncology, immunology and internal medicine, and became a founding partner (with GSK and Sanofi) in Parse and Nomic's Cascade immune-perturbation dataset. Neither deal has disclosed terms; both rent capability rather than take equity.

movers.player: Other big & mid-size pharma (Roche, GSK, Astellas, Zealand, Boehringer, UCB, Pierre Fabre)
movers.direction: Licensing AI design platforms across their pipelines rather than building them
movers.detail: Roche signed Chai (Nov 5) to use Chai-3 and its protein-design software across several discovery programs, a month after GSK widened its own Chai deal following lab tests; UCB signed Cradle (Nov 4), joining Bayer, Lundbeck and Hansa as Cradle customers this year. Astellas licensed AI Proteins' miniproteins (more than $400M), Zealand hired Generate for obesity proteins ($30M upfront), GSK joined the Cascade immune-data consortium, and Boehringer went to Microsoft for trial twins. Pierre Fabre added XtalPi on Nov 9 for de novo small molecules in oncology, on undisclosed terms.

movers.direction: Consolidating its own AI platforms instead of funding them separately
movers.detail: Flagship merged Cellarity, Etiome and Empress (together $374M raised) into Etcelera with no new capital disclosed, spun Cellarity's sickle cell drug into its own company, and is lining up a big-pharma alliance for the combined platform.
Lightspeed led Warp's $215M launch and is reportedly in talks to lead Miles Wang's ~$200M round.

movers.direction: Owning the make-and-test layer end to end
movers.detail: Lux is in Warp (automated chemistry) and Multiply Labs (robotic manufacturing), and earlier this autumn backed Enveda (AI natural-product discovery, now clinical).

Creandum led Atlas Bio's $10M seed, HV Capital led Rivercell's €22M seed, AVP led WhiteLab's $26M Series B, Asabys led ALLOX's $10.5M seed and PXN Ventures led adsilico's £10M Series A, so European funds are writing larger early cheques for data-first AI biology and virtual-patient simulation. Greek-American Kos Biotechnology Partners took its first AI-discovery stake on Nov 6, joining Fathom's US Series A. Astanor led Biomatter's $18M Series A on Nov 12, with UVC Partners adding to its stake, for AI enzyme design that already has paying customers. On Nov 12 Norrsken VC and Singular co-led Orakl Oncology's $34M Series A for organoid-based trial prediction, with Bpifrance's Patient Autonome Fund among new backers, and Treehouse Delmar put $5M into Switchpoint Bio's blood-biomarker pre-seed on Nov 11.

movers.direction: Positioning for AI-biotech IPOs, late rounds and data partnerships
movers.detail: ARK and Duquesne indicated about 40% of Iambic's IPO, ARK, Janus Henderson and Driehaus took part in Recursion's $200M follow-on, CPP Investments is in Hexagon's Series C, the UK's Sovereign AI fund co-led Potential Sciences' seed and added supercomputer time, the Abu Dhabi Investment Council and Duke's endowment joined Biossil's $153M round, Abu Dhabi is offering its health data to AI drug companies, and the US Energy Department pledged more than $500M over five years to Biohub's open cell-data effort.

movers.direction: Funding domestic AI protein design at $100M scale
movers.detail: China Life Capital led BioGeometry's Series A+, taking its Series A past $100M, with China Development Venture Capital and the Shanghai biomedical fund alongside; the company targets bispecific antibody INDs in 2027. Hong Kong is adding a partnership track: BioMap, hosted with support from the Hong Kong Investment Corporation, announced ten named collaborations on Nov 12 (HKU, Harbour BioMed, Revvity, Temasek Life Sciences Laboratory and others) with no disclosed money.

movers.direction: Funding AI-run drug development asset by asset, not company by company
movers.detail: Unnamed research foundations, endowments, hospitals and philanthropies committed $600M to Formation Bio's first fund, which buys Phase 1–2 drugs into standalone companies. It is the first time this kind of non-venture money has backed an AI drug developer at this scale.

movers.direction: Buying AI-designed molecules from Chinese platforms to seed its own companies
movers.detail: Third Rock committed up to about $2.16B, with an undisclosed platform fee upfront, for Funnel Biosciences to design antibodies against targets it nominates; it is the firm's second such deal with a Chinese AI designer after a peptide pact with Perpetual Medicine that has already produced a development candidate. A venture firm acting like a pharma licensee is new on this map.

Clinical-stage AI: Formation Bio's first fund-backed in-licensing deals, Biossil reopening the WashU SYN-004 trial and its next asset buys, a first program credited to Edison's Kosmos at Pfizer, whether AstraZeneca–Oracle becomes binding, Unlearn's digital-twin poster for Structure's aleniglipron at ObesityWeek (Nov 14–17), and whether Orakl turns its Sanofi asset work or its 18-of-top-20 pharma talks into a disclosed contract

items.summary: Orakl, a 2023 spin-out of Paris cancer centre Gustave Roussy, tests drugs on lab-grown copies of patients' tumours and combines the readouts with clinical records to train models that forecast how a drug will do in trials. It closed an oversubscribed $34M Series A co-led by Norrsken VC and Singular, taking total funding to $50M.
items.why_invested: Norrsken framed the bet around the cost of sending cancer drugs into trials without knowing who will respond, and pointed to Orakl's mix of patient data, hospital ties and its own lab as hard to copy; Singular, which led the seed, backed the founding team's blend of oncology, cell biology and computation.
items.whats_next: Five times more organoid data, new lung and gastric cancer models beyond colorectal and pancreatic, and US and UK teams to run predictions on more than 10 drug programs. The test that matters is the four Sanofi oncology assets it took on in July; its headline accuracy comes from a retrospective, not yet peer-reviewed preprint on mostly standard chemotherapy, so watch for a prospective readout on newer drugs and a first paid pharma contract (it says 18 of the top 20 are in talks).
items.why_it_matters: European venture money is now funding AI that predicts trial outcomes from patient-derived biology, adding a wet-lab, oncology flavour to the digital-twin and trial-simulation bets that dominated October.

items.summary: Vilnius-based Biomatter designs enzymes from the chemistry of the reaction a customer needs, instead of tweaking natural enzymes, and feeds each project's lab results back into its models. It closed an oversubscribed $18M Series A led by Astanor, and says it has delivered more than 50 custom enzymes to over 25 companies, among them AstraZeneca, Sanofi and BASF.
items.why_invested: UVC Partners raised its stake because Biomatter's enzymes already ship inside manufacturers' products while most AI-biology companies are still proving their methods; Astanor pointed to years of proprietary data on enzymes that don't exist in nature and to repeat customers.
items.whats_next: A roughly 2,000 m² design-and-testing site in Vilnius in 2027, meant to cut design cycles from weeks to days, plus a bigger commercial team and US presence (about half its customers are American). Watch for a named pharma manufacturing deal or a royalty-bearing enzyme in a drug process.
items.why_it_matters: Investors are paying for AI protein design that already earns revenue in manufacturing, and the money again goes into an in-house lab to generate the next round of training data.

items.summary: Unlearn, which builds AI 'digital twins' that forecast how a trial patient would have done untreated, will run its models over data from Structure Therapeutics' completed open-label extension study of aleniglipron, an oral GLP-1 pill. The modelled untreated outcomes are compared with what patients actually did; no financial terms were given.
items.why_invested: Structure says the analysis sits outside its formal development program but could add context on aleniglipron's longer-term profile, which matters when an open-label extension has no placebo group to compare against. Likely: an oral GLP-1 developer wants every extra piece of evidence it can get against injectable rivals.
items.whats_next: Results come as a poster at ObesityWeek, Nov 14–17 in National Harbor, Maryland. Watch whether Structure or another obesity developer uses Unlearn's twins prospectively in a registrational trial, where the EMA-qualified method could shrink a control arm.
items.why_it_matters: Digital twins are moving from pilot deals with big pharma into the crowded obesity race, used here to fill in the missing control group of an extension study.

items.summary: Helsinki- and Cambridge-based Switchpoint Bio, just out of stealth, reads DNA methylation in circulating immune cells from routine blood draws and uses AI to interpret how a patient's biology shifts during treatment, in place of repeat biopsies. It raised a $5.3M pre-seed, $5M of it from Treehouse Delmar Investments.
items.why_invested: Treehouse Delmar described a long-horizon bet on science that could change how disease is understood; likely also: drug developers want cheap, repeatable readouts of who responds and why, which a blood-based assay could supply across a trial.
items.whats_next: Clinical and industry validation, larger clinical and biobank datasets, and a first test in autoimmune disease starting with lupus; it is discussing first validation programs with drug developers, so watch for a named pharma or biotech pilot.
items.why_it_matters: A small but clear sign that trial-stage AI money is reaching the biomarker layer: models that explain response inside a trial, not just predict outcomes before it.

items.summary: Fauna Bio, which mines the genomes of hundreds of mammal species, including hibernators, for drug targets, named a second obesity target under its 2023 collaboration with Eli Lilly. The target sits in a different tissue from the first one, which was designated in March, and was picked by its Convergence AI platform; the milestone triggers an undisclosed payment.
items.why_invested: Likely: Lilly is buying a different route to obesity targets than the incretin biology its franchise rests on, using animals that gain and shed weight naturally each year. Fauna frames the second hit as proof that its platform can repeat, not a one-off.
items.whats_next: The release gives no timeline. Watch whether Lilly moves either target into a named drug program, which would trigger larger development milestones from the up-to-$494M pool, and whether Fauna uses the momentum to raise or sign a second pharma partner.
items.why_it_matters: Older AI-target deals signed in 2023 are now paying out in steps, which is the evidence pharma needs before the next round of platform licences.

items.summary: Boltz, the public-benefit company behind the open Boltz structure models, is using Excelra's curated GOSTAR database of measured solubility, lipophilicity and Caco-2 permeability to train the ADMET models in its BoltzMol-1 product. No financial terms were given; the companies say models trained on the data matched or beat a leading open-source ADMET tool on unfamiliar chemistry.
items.why_invested: Stated: Boltz says curated measurements at this scale help its models generalise far outside typical training chemistry and save it time; Excelra argues public sources lack enough curated solubility data. Likely: Boltz needs proprietary-grade property data to sell a commercial filtering product on top of its open models.
items.whats_next: No timeline was given. Watch whether Boltz publishes benchmark numbers beyond the release's claims, signs more data suppliers, and whether pharma customers such as Pfizer, already a Boltz partner, adopt BoltzMol-1 for compound triage.
items.why_it_matters: Even open-model companies now pay for curated experimental data, so the edge in molecular property prediction is shifting to whoever owns clean measurements.

Watch its brain-penetrant ATR inhibitor data at the Society for Neuro-Oncology meeting.

items.area: Autonomous lab for human cells and organoids
items.summary: iORGANBIO, a North Carolina startup founded in 2024, makes human cells and organoids that drug companies use to test candidates, running production through a closed loop of AI, single-cell analysis and robotics. Mitsui Chemicals invested through its 321Catalyst venture fund on undisclosed terms, and the two will work together on culture conditions using Mitsui's materials and its InnoCell plates.
items.why_invested: Likely: Mitsui gets a showcase and a data feedback loop for its cell-culture materials inside an automated cell factory, plus a stake in human-cell models that could stand in for some animal testing. The release frames the work around better cell uniformity and cell types that have been hard to produce.
items.whats_next: The companies say only that they will explore joint development, with no timelines, milestones or definitive agreements. Watch for named pharma customers, organoid-based safety or efficacy assays, and whether a priced round follows this strategic cheque.
items.why_it_matters: Closed-loop automation is spreading from chemistry and protein testing into making the human cells drugs are tested on, and materials suppliers are now buying positions in it.

items.why_invested: Stated by Raoof: pharma has long outsourced development services, and AI can deliver much of that work faster and cheaper, a pattern he compares to AI in legal and finance services. Likely for the LPs: SignalFire and Kleiner get early sight of companies they could lead later, and the Dimension founders and former FDA official Amy Abernethy add regulatory and techbio networks.
items.whats_next: Watch the remaining portfolio names as they are disclosed, which services they target (CRO work, regulatory writing, trial operations), and whether SignalFire or Kleiner lead their Series A rounds. Not counted in the venture total because it is fund capital, not money raised by a company.
items.why_it_matters: Specialist seed money is now forming around AI for the unglamorous development-services layer rather than molecule design, matching Formation Bio's and Biossil's bet that the bottleneck is downstream.

items.summary: argenx agreed to buy the rest of Santa Cruz-based Unnatural Products for $550M in cash plus up to $595M in development and regulatory milestones. The target combines machine learning with massively parallel synthesis and direct-to-biology screening to make macrocyclic peptides that can be taken orally.
items.why_invested: argenx says the peptide chemistry complements its antibody engineering and gives it a route to oral and long-acting immunology medicines. It had more than two years of collaboration data before buying, and joined the target's $45M Series B in March. A Leerink analyst read the move as longer-term pipeline diversification.
items.whats_next: Closing is expected by the end of 2026, subject to customary conditions. Santa Cruz becomes argenx's peptide discovery hub. No named programs or clinic dates have been given. Watch what happens to Unnatural Products' other partnerships (Novartis, Merck & Co., BridgeBio) under a new owner, and whether oral delivery clears the known permeability and gut-stability hurdles for this drug class.
items.why_it_matters: A buyer that had seen the platform's results from the inside paid about 48% of the headline value in cash up front, far above the 2–3% typical of AI discovery licences, which suggests pharma pays real money once a design-and-make loop is proven on its own targets.

items.area: Causal virtual cell plus patient genomics
items.summary: Paris-based DeepLife, whose TwinCell causal cell model is built on single-cell multi-omics data, signed a co-development deal with KOSDAQ-listed Korean genomics company 3billion to find small molecules against genetic modifiers, the genes that change how severely a disease shows up in people carrying the same mutation. No financial terms were disclosed.
items.why_invested: Stated: each side holds half of the path. DeepLife's model nominates causal targets, 3billion checks them against the genomes from its rare-disease testing business, which the release puts at more than 110,000 people, and designs compounds with its own AI chemistry tools. Modifier targets offer a way in when the disease gene itself resists drugging.
items.whats_next: The partners plan to carry programs through preclinical and IND-enabling work and then license them to larger pharma. No indications, timelines or milestones were named. Watch for a first disclosed target and whether a pharma partner joins.
items.why_it_matters: Two mid-size AI companies are pooling a virtual-cell model with a proprietary patient-genome cohort to own the assets themselves, a sign that data holders outside big pharma would rather take a stake in drugs than sell access.

items.why_invested: Kos says it is betting that simulation-plus-AI raises discovery productivity and opens targets that static-structure methods cannot reach; earlier backers include Lilly Ventures, which ties a large pharma to the approach.
items.whats_next: Fathom hired Bret Williams (ex-Magnet Biomedicine, Relay, Sanofi) as CSO on Oct 29 to turn Microcosmos designs into named programs, so watch for its first disclosed targets, a first pharma partnership, and a Series B once programs reach candidate stage.

Likely: Third Rock wants de novo antibodies for hard targets to seed its own new companies, sourced from a fast, lower-cost Chinese design shop rather than built in-house.

Watch for the first development candidate (Third Rock's earlier peptide pact with Shanghai's Perpetual Medicine produced one in under 18 months), a Third Rock company launched around a Funnel antibody, Funnel's own first financing, and any US scrutiny of China-sourced biologics.

items.summary: Venomics AI, a Bengaluru spinout of the Indian Institute of Science, sequences animal-venom molecules into a dataset it calls the Venom Atlas, ranks candidates with AI and checks them in its own lab screens. It closed a $2.7M pre-seed, its first institutional round, co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons.
items.why_invested: Likely: the backers are buying a proprietary dataset in a largely untapped chemical space, where a closed loop of AI ranking and wet-lab testing can turn venom peptides into drug leads that public data cannot reach.
items.whats_next: The money goes to growing the Venom Atlas, building out AI and lab screening, hiring across venom biology and computation, and validating its first leads. Watch for a named lead program or a first pharma or biodefense partner.
items.why_it_matters: Even at pre-seed, investors back the data-first model: a small team wins funding by owning an unusual dataset plus the lab to generate more of it, the same logic behind ALLOX, Rivercell and the larger cell-data coalitions.

items.whats_next: Chai's tools go into multiple Roche programs. Watch for disclosed terms, whether Genentech is included, the first Roche program credited to Chai designs, and a new Chai raise on the back of its partner list.

items.why_invested: Sovereign AI says it wants the company to become a frontier lab for chemistry and is adding compute on the Isambard-AI supercomputer; the company's pitch is that AI chemistry models are short of good data and that physics-based calculation could cut the cost of that data by about 100x.
items.whats_next: Use of funds was not detailed. Watch for its first model release or benchmarks, a first pharma or materials partner, and how much Isambard-AI compute it is allotted.
items.why_it_matters: A third answer to biology's data shortage is getting funded: alongside open coalitions (Biohub) and pharma-shared datasets (Cascade), investors are now backing startups that generate training data by simulation, with the UK state backing it directly.

No new clinical data has been disclosed to justify the step-up, so this is a platform bet.

items.summary: Toronto-based Biossil, an AI-native company that hunts for shelved drug candidates and develops them itself, agreed to buy Theriva Biologics' antibiotic-degrading enzyme portfolio, led by SYN-004 (ribaxamase), plus SYN-007 and SYN-006-related assets. items.why_invested: Likely: the asset fits Biossil's model of buying molecules that stalled for business reasons rather than failed on biology, here a Phase 1b/2a enzyme meant to protect the gut microbiome of stem-cell transplant patients. Theriva says the sale keeps the program alive while it focuses on its oncolytic virus VCN-01. The near-zero upfront shows the seller had little leverage.
items.whats_next: Biossil plans to restart the paused Washington University Phase 1b/2a trial in allogeneic transplant patients (two of three cohorts done, with a third planned on IV cefepime, up to 36 evaluable patients). Watch for the trial reopening, and for more cheap buys of shelved assets with the $153M it raised in September.
items.why_it_matters: OpenAI-backed capital is now flowing through AI-native developers into the clinic by buying shelved assets for almost nothing upfront, the same play Formation Bio is funding with $600M.

items.whats_next: Building its AI hotspot models, growing the in-house chemistry team, moving several programs toward small-molecule candidates and signing pharma research partnerships.

items.summary: Brooklyn-founded Opentrons sells open, low-cost liquid-handling robots (Flex and OT-2) that AI systems can drive to design, run and adjust experiments in a loop. It has more than 11,000 robots in over 80 countries and raised a $40M Series E led by healthcare investor Avego.

Likely also: the installed base gives a cheap route to selling AI software and data tools on top of hardware already in place.
items.whats_next: Spend on AI-driven experiment execution, faster protocol writing through software and AI, tighter links to other lab instruments, and new regions. Watch for agent or model integrations (e.g. with frontier AI labs) and whether the smaller round, well below its $200M SoftBank-led Series C in 2021, signals a flat or lower valuation.

items.summary: Formation Bio, the New York AI-native drug developer that works with Sanofi and OpenAI, closed $600M in commitments for its first fund, the Drug Development Accelerator Fund. The fund will only finance Phase 1 and 2 drugs Formation buys or in-licenses, each held in its own company. No LPs were named.
items.why_invested: Stated: LPs get exposure to single drug programs without funding a whole biotech, and Formation gets cheaper capital, more programs and ways to cash out without selling the parent. Its bet is that the bottleneck is pushing stalled clinical drugs through trials, not finding molecules. Likely: mission-driven LPs (foundations, hospitals) like the focus on neglected diseases with little active development.

items.why_invested: The partners say no single group can generate enough standardized cell data to build an accurate model of how cells respond to drugs or genetic changes, so they are pooling it. Likely also for the tech companies: early exclusive access to the data (reported at one year before public release) feeds their own biology models, including Isomorphic's drug design engine.
items.whats_next: Watch for the first released datasets, how the one-year commercial head start works in practice, which other companies buy in, and whether DOE's autonomous labs start producing data at scale. Note that the new money named is closer to $1.3B; the rest is prior NIH investment.
items.why_it_matters: Big tech is now paying for the raw data layer of biology, not just models, which raises the bar for startups whose edge is a proprietary cell atlas.

items.summary: Paris-based WhiteLab uses its ALFRED platform to design delivery vehicles for genomic medicines, including AAV capsids that crossed the blood-brain barrier in animal work with the Paris Brain Institute. AVP led a $26M Series B.
items.why_invested: Likely: investors are backing evidence that AI-designed capsids work in living animals, plus the novel sequences that could make for defensible IP; the company pitches better brain delivery for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.
items.whats_next: In vivo validation of viral and non-viral delivery (including LNPs) and synthetic promoters, building a portfolio of bio-assets to keep or partner, and expansion to the US, Japan and South Korea. Watch for a first pharma licensing deal.
items.why_it_matters: Delivery is becoming its own AI-design category, alongside the Lilly–METiS deal.

items.summary: Biossil, which uses language models to find drug candidates that pharma dropped after clinical setbacks and then buys or licenses them, raised $153M at a reported $1B valuation, five months after leaving stealth with $70M. BetaKit reports the OpenAI Startup Fund led; The Logic lists OpenAI among the backers without naming a lead.
items.why_invested: The CEO's stated case is that AI insight only helps patients if a company has the clinical infrastructure to act on it. Likely: OpenAI wants a showcase where its models drive real drug programs, and backers see shelved assets as cheaper and faster to develop than new discovery.
items.whats_next: Funds go to clinical development capacity in the US and Canada and to buying more candidates; its first public buy came Nov 2 (Theriva's SYN-004 enzymes). Current work spans sickle cell, IPF, glioblastoma, breast cancer and Alzheimer's. Watch for further asset deals and trial starts.
items.why_it_matters: AI-lab money is backing companies that own clinical assets, not just discovery software.
